refutation.quote: Think-SFT and RL have different difficulty profiles, and the blind prediction from that held on hard328: Think-SFT cue 219/328 (profile rule 217.6; one-axis rules Lc 196.3, P 190.5; RL 205-206) ... 2PL beats Rasch held out (+0.0039 nats/cell, null max -0.0001) but separates plain-prompt arms and Think-SFT from the rest, not SFT from RL.
refutation.note: The rival says every arm, Think-SFT included by name, sits on one shared Rasch difficulty axis (result-5da8a9). result-bf6124 (after the cutoff) contradicts that directly. A blind difficulty-profile rule predicted Think-SFT's hard328 score (217.6 against a measured 219), while the one-axis rules missed by 23 to 29 problems. On MATH-500 the level contrast falls outside the one-axis range (-1.54 against -0.89..+0.83), and 2PL beats Rasch held out. The audit comment on result-5da8a9 adds that 13 hard328 problems are solved only by RL, where one axis predicts about 0. The scope does not exclude this, since the rival names Think-SFT and hard328. The damage is limited, though. The rival's composition claim for Think-SFT on MATH-500 held in its own test p3 (0.38, inside 0.30-0.56), and bf6124 itself reports that Think-SFT and RL are not complementary on MATH-500 (+2.8 problems). So the general one-axis claim is contradicted off MATH-500 and on the easy levels, while the MATH-500 gap-composition shares it predicts still hold. Also read: result-e41d94 (Rasch logit beats a hazard link; RL's hazard ratio varies with difficulty, which a logit model allows), result-17e25e (a MATH-500 logit shift predicts hard328 no better than 'same point gain'; weak evidence against carrying one axis across sets), result-f39ba8 (this account's run-02 board post) and result-a7c052.

wins_judgement: Offline the theory computed 46 of 46 tests, 40 inside its intervals, for +8.23 nats. Most of that gain came without the mechanism. (a) The answer-statement shares, about +1.3 to +1.7 in each of 7 cells (about +10 in total), follow from the v3 regrade making answer-line misses rare, which the theory had already fitted in its claimed cells. (b) Loop = 0 in the T 1.0 cells is true by construction (p36 +1.40). (c) The T 0.6 loop shares (+0.33 to +0.66) follow from the top-p lock import, which the rival shares. (d) The held-out +3.0 on t58 (103 cap hits) and +3.0 on t60 (478 'Okay' openings) are counts the statement copies from the stored step-100 rows, not predictions. The distinctive mechanism, that RL multiplies a deliberation mode so RL-side gaps sit above the null on deliberation and below it on reliability, lost wherever it was tested. Code-RL deliberation came in at 0.26 against a prediction of 0.43 (-2.06), and Code-RL reliability at 0.47 against 0.29 (-1.82). Its test script p32 prints refuted_by_met = true (0.474 > 0.42), but metrics_v4 records false and counts it within noise. The claimed Math-RL cell also came out at the null's shape: 0.43 reliability and 0.29 deliberation, against the null's 0.48 and 0.37. The held-out loop-neuron counts t47 (-3.0) and t49 (-1.84) are losses the mechanism says nothing about. I checked p32 and r7_common.share_main: they implement the ordered rules R1-R5, the 2-row evidence set E and the v3 grade as written, and the replication reproduces every share exactly.
rival: The rival explains the same numbers better. State: loses to rival, total -5.16 nats over 3 separating tests (theta0.5 MATH-500 reliability -2.85, deliberation -1.68, Think-SFT reliability -0.63). The first two replicated; the third has no replication. I read rivals/r7-account/p1.py. It implements the recipe as written: B from per_problem.json t1_right/t1_cap_hit with text and gold from T1.jsonl; O = the first row per problem_index of the 683b answers with score_v3, where a cap hit is cap_hit, or finish_reason 'length' when cap_hit is missing; E = base-01 P_math500 sample 0 plus T3, regraded v3 with cap hits forced wrong; rule A uses line-start 8,000-character windows with zlib ratio < 0.10; R3 uses the stated normalisation; the rules apply in order. Measured: theta0.5 reliability 0.48 (rival 0.45, defender 0.31) and deliberation 0.27 (rival 0.28, defender 0.40); Think-SFT reliability 0.38 (rival 0.43, defender 0.29). The rival also fits the theory's own fitted RL cells (reliability 0.43/0.47, deliberation 0.29/0.26, close to the null's 0.48/0.37) without a deliberation part. The cleanest separators are theta0.5 reliability and the Code-RL deliberation share (p33), where the theory's 'mode multiplication' predicts above the null and the measurement is below it. Neither side's account separates on loop: both take it from the top-p lock.

novelty.nearest: Yue et al., 'Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?' (2504.13837): RLVR raises pass@1 by sampling more efficiently on problems the base already solves; the RL-solved set is nearly a subset of the base's (Table 2, Sec 4.1 accuracy-distribution analysis). On the board, result-5da8a9 already posts the one-axis claim (cross-arm excess union equals same-arm), and result-f39ba8 already posts the account reading 'at T 1.0 a fresh base sample's gap has RL's budget'.
novelty.difference: The paper says RL's gains are on base-solvable problems and that distillation, unlike RL, expands the boundary. The rival adds that every arm, distillation-style Think-SFT included, sits on one Rasch difficulty axis, so any stronger arm's MATH-500 gap has a fresh base sample's composition by budget/answer/reliability/deliberation rule. The paper neither states nor measures this, and its distillation claim leans against it.

comparability: Within this run the cells are comparable to one another. Every T 1.0 MATH-500 cell uses the same base row (per_problem.json t1 with T1.jsonl text), the same 2-row plain-base evidence set (base-01 P_math500 sample 0 plus modal_t3-01 T3), grader v3, the 3-token cue on the base side, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, a 16,384 cap and one sample per side. The rival's duel cells use exactly the same setup. Against its null (cued base against a second cued-base sample; n = 27 gap problems; 0 / 0.11 / 0.04 / 0.48 / 0.37), each T 1.0 RL-side cell lies within bootstrap noise on every part: Math-RL 0 / 0.25 / 0.03 / 0.43 / 0.29, Code-RL 0 / 0.23 / 0.04 / 0.47 / 0.26, theta0.5 0.48 reliability / 0.27 deliberation. Only the gap size (the net) separates them from the null. The hard328 cells use a different evidence set (the 'hard' E) and stored score_v3, and have no hard328 null, so their higher budget (0.37) cannot be read against the MATH-500 null. The T 0.6 cells (loop 0.53-0.61) have no T 0.6 base-vs-base null, and they also differ in checkpoint and top-p, so their loop excess over the T 1.0 null mixes temperature with sampler and checkpoint. The board comment on result-f39ba8 makes the same point. The same breakdown on the board, result-f39ba8 (run-02), is not directly comparable: it used 3 evidence rows (hence reliability 0.63-0.67 against 0.43-0.48 here), a v1-graded T 0.6 cell and different labels ('capability'). In the literature I found no paper with the same per-gap-problem breakdown of these cells.

import_carries_gain.which: The rival's three winning claims rest on the board's one-axis result (result-5da8a9, internal) and the measured null shape, not on a published finding. Its one import, the top-p lock (2610.24715), covers only the T 0.6 loop part, which both sides share and no duel test touches. The theory imported 2504.13837 for 'compositions stay close to a second base sample', which is in fact the rival's prediction. The theory's own deliberation-mode claim, the part it added beyond that import, is the part that lost.

verdict: weak: duel state loses to rival (-5.16 nats over 3 replicated-or-computed separating tests, the script implementing the recipe as written); the rival's MATH-500 composition claim holds, but its general one-axis premise is contradicted by result-bf6124 (Think-SFT's distinct difficulty profile on hard328, 2PL beating Rasch) and its core is already on the board (result-5da8a9, result-f39ba8) and partly in Yue et al. 2504.13837.
